UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                   BEFORE THE
                     FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


                                                 )
           PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et.al.   )                  Docket Nos. EL25-49-000
                                                 )                              EL25-49-001
                                                 )
           Large Loads Co-Locating at Generating )                                   AD24-11-000
           Facilities                            )
                                                 )
           Constellation Energy Generation, LLC )
           v.                                    )                                   EL25-20-000
           PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.           )                                   (Consolidated)
                                                 )


         REPLY BRIEF OF ADVANCED ENERGY UNITED AND THE SOLAR ENERGY
                            INDUSTRIES ASSOCIATION


    I.     Introduction

           Pursuant to paragraph 219 and ordering paragraphs (D) and (E) of the Order on Show

Cause Proceeding (“Co-Location Order”) Directing Compliance Filings, Establishing Paper

Hearing, and Granting in Part and Denying in Part Complaint issued by the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission (“Commission”) on December 18, 2025,1 Advanced Energy United




1
 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 193 FERC ¶ 61,217, at P 219 and Ordering Paragraphs (D) and (E) (2025) (“Co-
Location Order”)
 (“United”)2 and the Solar Energy Industries Association (“SEIA”)3 submit this brief in reply to

PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) February 23, 2026, Initial Brief (“PJM Brief”).4

         The Commission issued the Co-Location Order in response to an unprecedented surge in

requests to interconnect large co-located loads—most notably hyperscale data centers and

advanced manufacturing facilities—to generating facilities within the PJM Interconnection

region. The Commission found that PJM’s existing tariff was unjust and unreasonable because it

lacked service options that allow customers to flexibly manage their withdrawals from the

transmission system, and lacked clarity and consistency in the rates, terms, and conditions

applicable to co-located load arrangements.5 The Commission recognized that the absence of a

clear, accessible regulatory framework was itself a barrier to the rapid integration of new load,

with significant consequences for reliability and economic development. The Commission

therefore directed PJM to develop three new transmission services as permanent and transitional

alternatives to existing Network Integration Transmission Service (“NITS”) for Eligible

Customers serving co-located loads that are willing and able to control their withdrawals from

the transmission system: Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service, Non-Firm Contract

Demand Transmission Service, and Interim Network Integration Transmission Service (“Interim

NITS”).6




2
  Advanced Energy United is a national association of businesses that are making the energy we use secure,
clean and affordable. Advanced Energy United is the only industry association in the United States that represents
the full range of advanced energy technologies and services, both grid-scale and distributed. Advanced energy
includes energy efficiency, demand response, energy storage, wind, solar, hydro, nuclear, electric vehicles, and
more. The comments expressed in this filing represent the position of Advanced Energy United but may not
represent the views of any particular member.
3
  The comments contained in this filing represent the position of SEIA as a trade organization on behalf of the solar
industry, but do not necessarily reflect the views of any particular member with respect to any issue.
4
  PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Initial Brief of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. EL25-49-000 (Feb. 23,
2026) (“PJM Brief”).
5
  Co-Location Order at P 2.
6
  Id.


                                                          2
            PJM submitted its initial brief on February 23, 2026, setting forth illustrative tariff

language and responding to the Commission's paper hearing questions on the non-rate terms and

conditions of the three new transmission services. While PJM's proposed framework represents a

meaningful attempt to address the novel operational and reliability challenges associated with co-

located load, PJM’s initial brief falls short of the Co-Location Order's requirements in several

important respects that, if left unaddressed, would produce a framework unlikely to achieve the

Commission's objectives.

           First, PJM’s proposed Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service departs

materially from the Commission's directives by restricting the service to periods when the co-

located generating facility is on outage. This converts a service the Commission designed as a

flexible, as-available option during normal operating conditions into a narrow standby product.

The Commission was explicit: Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service “must be

available during normal operations,” with reservations available “as needed during normal, non-

emergency system operating conditions.”7 PJM’s illustrative tariff contradicts this by limiting

eligibility to obtain the service “only to the extent the portion of the Co-Located Generating

Facility dedicated to serving the Co-Located Load is on outage.”8 The Commission should reject

this restriction and direct PJM to implement Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service

consistent with the Co-Location Order.

           Second, PJM’s curtailment framework fails to provide sufficient transparency for

prospective customers to make informed commercial decisions about whether to take Interim

NITS or Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service. PJM has offered no meaningful

information about the expected frequency or duration of curtailment under real system


7
    Id. at P 215.
8
    PJM Brief Attachment A, Illustrative Language for New Tariff, Part XI, Section 709.2 (b).


                                                           3
 conditions. Moreover, PJM's curtailment language is internally inconsistent—using “may” to

describe curtailment before pre-emergency demand response in one instance and “will” in

another—introducing ambiguity that must be resolved.9 Without greater transparency and

certainty, curtailment risk will suppress participation in these new services and frustrate the

Commission’s goals.

           Third, while appropriate study of co-located generating facilities is necessary to protect

transmission system reliability, PJM’s proposal to subject all co-located generating facilities,

including those that have no intention of ever exporting power to the grid, to the full PJM

interconnection queue process is unnecessarily burdensome and inconsistent with the Co-

Location Order’s speed-to-power objectives. The interconnection queue was designed to study

the deliverability and system impacts of exporting generators; applying it wholesale to non-

exporting resources that will serve only their co-located load imposes multi-year delays and costs

that are disproportionate to any reliability benefit and would further burden an interconnection

queue that is already significantly backlogged, to the detriment of the broader PJM region. The

Commission should direct PJM to develop a streamlined study and registration pathway for non-

exporting co-located generating facilities that provides PJM with the operational visibility it

needs without subjecting these resources to the full burdens of the interconnection queue.

           Fourth, PJM’s framework fails to honor the Co-Location Order’s directive that co-located

loads curtailed from grid service under Interim NITS must be permitted to continue taking

energy directly from their co-located generating facility. The Commission stated that “when

curtailed, Eligible Customers taking this transmission service on behalf of Co-Located Loads

may be able to continue to take energy from the Interconnection Customer with which they are



9
    PJM Initial Brief at 63-64


                                                    4
 co-located if PJM’s Tariff otherwise allows.”10 This is the foundational commercial rationale for

co-location with a new generating facility, and denying it directly conflicts with the Co-Location

Order’s speed-to-power objectives.

           The Commission should direct PJM to revise its proposed terms and conditions to: (1)

make Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service available during normal operating

conditions, not solely during generating facility outages; (2) provide greater transparency

regarding curtailment triggers and frequency, and resolve the ambiguity in its curtailment

priority language; (3) establish a streamlined study and registration pathway for non-exporting

co-located generating facilities in lieu of the full interconnection queue process; and (4) confirm

that Eligible Customers taking Interim NITS may continue to take energy from their co-located

generating facility during curtailment periods, so long as there are no net injections or

withdrawals from the co-located facility, consistent with the Co-Location Order.


     II.   REPLY AND PROTEST

               A. PJM’s Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service Inverts the
                  Commission’s Intent

           The Commission directed PJM to develop Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission

Service as a permanent transmission service option available to Eligible Customers seeking

flexible, as-available access to the transmission system on behalf of co-located loads during

normal operating conditions.11 PJM’s proposed implementation of this service departs materially

from that directive by restricting its availability to periods when the co-located generating




10
     Co-Location Order at P 201.
11
     Id. at P 215.


                                                  5
 facility is on outage.12 This restriction inverts the Commission’s intent, renders the service

commercially unworkable for the loads it was designed to serve, and must be rejected.

        The Commission’s directive on Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service is

unambiguous. In the Co-Location Order, the Commission stated:

                 We find that the new Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission
                 service must be available during normal operations and curtailed
                 during emergency operations (i.e., it will be curtailed before existing
                 firm transmission services and the new Firm Contract Demand
                 Transmission Service). Under this service, Eligible Customers may
                 reserve transmission service on behalf of a Co-Located Load as
                 needed during normal, non-emergency system operating conditions.
                 Reservations under this service would be available only when there
                 is available transmission capacity, similar to existing non-firm
                 transmission service options in the Tariff.13

The Commission further specified that reservations under Non-Firm Contract Demand

Transmission Service “shall be available for terms ranging from one hour to one month,

consistent with the terms available for Non-Firm PTPS in the PJM Tariff.”14 The reference to

Non-Firm Point-to-Point Transmission Service (“Non-Firm PTPS”) is instructive: Non-Firm

PTPS is available on an as-available basis during normal system conditions across a range of

reservation periods, and is not limited to any particular triggering event such as a generator

outage as is required in PJM’s proposed tariffs.15 The Commission’s reference to Non-Firm

PTPS makes clear that Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service must function as a

flexible, broadly available service option, not a narrow emergency backstop.

        After explaining that there are situations in which Co-Located Loads may withdraw

energy from the transmission system from time to time when transmission capacity is available,


12
   PJM Brief Attachment A, Illustrative Language for New Tariff, Part XI, Section 709.2(b).
13
   Co-Location Order at P 215.
14
   Id.
15
   PJM Brief Attachment A, Illustrative Language for New Tariff, Part XI, Section 709.2(b).


                                                        6
 the Commission provided an illustrative example of how Non-Firm Contract Demand

Transmission Service might be used: “an Eligible Customer could seek a transmission

reservation for a Co-Located Load in advance for the duration of an expected outage of the

associated generator.”16 This example describes one likely and common use case. It does not

define or limit the circumstances under which the service may be available. That the

Commission offered one example of how the service might be used does not mean that example

defines the only circumstances under which the service is available. The Co-Location Order

contains no such limitation.

        Contrary to the Commission’s clear directive, PJM's illustrative tariff restricts Non-Firm

Contract Demand Transmission Service to a narrow set of circumstances that bear little

resemblance to the service the Commission ordered. Specifically, PJM proposes that “an Eligible

Customer with an effective Service Agreement will be eligible to obtain Non-Firm Contract

Demand Transmission Service on a given Operating Day only to the extent the portion of the Co-

Located Generating Facility dedicated to serving the Co-Located Load is on outage.”17 PJM

further characterizes the service as a “standby product” to be relied upon “under limited

circumstances,”18 and states that it “anticipates that in practice, requests for Non-Firm Contract

Demand Transmission Service will be at the MW level the Co-Located Generating Facility has

dedicated to serving the Co-Located Load,” available “only up to the MW level that the Co-

Located Generating Facility is on outage.”19

        This is not the service the Commission ordered. The Co-Location Order contemplated a

service available “as needed during normal, non-emergency system operating conditions,” a


16
   Co-Location Order at P 214.
17
   PJM Brief Attachment A, Illustrative Language for New Tariff, Part XI, Section 709.2(b).
18
   PJM Brief at 10.
19
   Id. at 32.


                                                        7
 standard that encompasses a wide range of circumstances in which a co-located load may wish to

draw supplemental energy from the transmission system, not merely periods of generator

unavailability. PJM has taken an illustrative example from the Co-Location Order and elevated it

into the governing rule, while discarding the broader principle the Commission established. This

approach is inconsistent with the Co-Location Order and must be rejected.

       The practical consequences of PJM's restriction are significant. Hybrid resources serving

co-located loads, including storage paired with solar and other technologies with variable or

intermittent output profiles, may require supplemental grid withdrawals not only during planned

outages but during any period in which the co-located generating facility’s output is constrained,

reduced, or otherwise insufficient to meet the full gross demand of the co-located load. Under

PJM's proposed framework, such a customer could not access Non-Firm Contract Demand

Transmission Service to cover that shortfall unless the generating facility is formally “on outage”

as defined in PJM’s tariff. This creates a significant gap in service availability that would force

many customers to take full NITS—with all of its associated costs and planning obligations—

simply to access the flexibility that Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service was

designed to provide.

       PJM's supporting testimony attempts to justify this restriction on operational and

planning complexity grounds, pointing to the challenges of designing protection systems that

adapt to varying system conditions and the risks of Remedial Action Scheme interactions in a

tightly coupled network. These concerns do not support PJM’s proposed limitation. The

Commission was fully aware that co-location arrangements would require novel operational

accommodations when it issued the Co-Location Order; PJM had raised precisely these




                                                  8
 protection scheme concerns as a reason to resist non-firm service,20 and the Commission directed

establishment of Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service, nonetheless, finding it “just

and reasonable.” 21 PJM's compliance filing is not the appropriate vehicle to relitigate that policy

judgment. To the extent PJM identifies genuine implementation constraints, the appropriate

response is a reasonable implementation timeline and clear Commission guidance on protection

system requirements, not a fundamental narrowing of the service itself. Notably, PJM’s own

testimony acknowledges that protection scheme solutions are workable in the core co-location

scenario: PJM witness Wharton concedes that a Remedial Action Scheme triggered by loss of the

co-located generating facility “would be overwhelmingly beneficial and would have a minimal

impact on the overall grid.”22 The Commission should reject this additional restriction as

inconsistent with the Co-Location Order's flexible service design.

        Moreover, from a resource adequacy and reliability perspective, there is no basis for

restricting Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service to outage periods. Non-Firm

Contract Demand Transmission Service is by design curtailed before firm transmission services

and before NITS in the curtailment hierarchy and is available only when transmission capacity

exists.23 These safeguards already ensure that Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service

does not displace higher-priority service or impose undue reliability burdens on the system.

Arbitrarily restricting availability to outage periods provides no additional reliability protection,

it simply reduces the utility of the service without any corresponding system benefit.

        PJM's proposed restriction of Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service to

generating facility outage periods is inconsistent with the Co-Location Order and must be


20
   “Answer of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.” Docket No. EL25-49-000 (March 24, 2025) at pages 13-15.
21
   Co-Location Order at P205 and 215.
22
   PJM Brief, Attachment C “Affidavit of Matthew Wharton on Behalf of PJM, Interconnection, L.L.C.” at P 25.
23
   Co-Location Order at P 215.


                                                       9
 rejected. The Commission should direct PJM to revise and file illustrative Tariff, Part XI,

Subpart B, section 709.2(b) to remove the outage-only limitation and replace it with language

consistent with the Co-Location Order's directive that the service be available as needed during

normal, non-emergency system operating conditions, subject to available transmission capacity

and the curtailment priority established in the Co-Location Order. This revision would restore the

service to the form the Commission intended: A flexible, as-available transmission option that

gives co-located loads a meaningful and commercially viable alternative to full NITS. The

Commission should find PJM’s outage-only restriction on Non-Firm Contract Demand

Transmission Service to be unjust and unreasonable and direct PJM to revise its illustrative tariff

accordingly.

               B. Additional Certainty Regarding Potential Curtailment is Needed to Enable
                  Uptake of the Non-Firm and Interim NITS Options

           The Commission directed PJM to create Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission

Service and Interim NITS to accommodate co-located load arrangements, and these services

must be genuinely accessible and commercially viable alternatives to full NITS for co-located

loads willing and able to limit their grid withdrawals.24 For these services to achieve that

purpose, prospective customers must be able to make informed business decisions about whether

to take service, and that requires a clear, consistent, and transparent curtailment framework.

PJM’s initial brief fails on both counts: it introduces internal inconsistency in the curtailment

priority hierarchy, and it provides no meaningful information about the conditions under which

curtailment will occur in practice. The Commission should direct PJM to resolve these

deficiencies before these services are implemented.




24
     Id at P214-215.


                                                 10
                  1. PJM's Curtailment Priority Language Is Internally Inconsistent and
                    Must Be Clarified

        The Co-Location Order established a clear curtailment hierarchy: Interim NITS and Non-

Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service are to be curtailed before firm transmission

services and existing NITS, and before pre-emergency demand response resources are

dispatched.25 This hierarchy is a critical feature of the new services, making them compatible

with system reliability and defining the conditions under which co-located loads can expect their

service to be interrupted.

        PJM’s Brief implements this hierarchy but does so in contradictory terms that must be

clarified and reconciled to confirm consistency with the Commission’s directive. In describing

curtailment procedures applicable to both Interim NITS and Non-Firm Contract Demand

Transmission Service, PJM states that “the Transmission Provider may also curtail Interim NITS

or Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service prior to dispatching the Pre-Emergency

Load Response Program.”26 Yet in the very next sentence, PJM states that “this effectively

means that Interim NITS and Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service will be curtailed

before Demand Response resources are called upon to reduce load.”27 PJM uses the same

contradictory language its discussion of the same curtailment trigger later in the brief when

discussing Interim NITS curtailment procedures.28

        This inconsistency may be unintentional but must be resolved. The difference between a

discretionary curtailment authority (“may”) and a mandatory curtailment obligation (“will”) has

material consequences for how co-located loads plan their operations and evaluate their



25
   Co-Location Order at P 215; see also PJM Brief at 63.
26
   PJM Brief at 63 (emphasis added).
27
   Id at 63-64.
28
   Id at 72.


                                                           11
 curtailment exposure. A customer deciding whether to take Non-Firm Contract Demand

Transmission Service or Interim NITS needs to know whether curtailment before pre-emergency

demand response is a certainty or a possibility. Likewise, demand response providers require

certainty as to how their obligations will be impacted by the new Non-Firm Contract Demand

Transmission Service and Interim NITS: Will customers on these non-firm services always be

curtailed prior to pre-emergency demand response? PJM's Brief answers both simultaneously

and inconsistently, leaving the customer no clearer on their actual exposure than before. The

Commission should direct PJM to resolve this inconsistency in its revised filing and confirm

unambiguously whether curtailment prior to pre-emergency demand response dispatch is

mandatory or discretionary.

               2. PJM's Curtailment Framework Provides Insufficient Transparency for
                  Customers to Make Informed Commercial Decisions

       Beyond the readily fixable “may/will” inconsistency, PJM’s curtailment framework

suffers from a deeper transparency problem: PJM has provided no information about the

conditions that would actually trigger curtailment of Interim NITS or Non-Firm Contract

Demand Transmission Service in practice. These are novel services for which no historical

curtailment data currently exists. There is no modeling of expected curtailment frequency or

duration under the proposed framework, and no examples of how the curtailment process would

operate for a hypothetical co-located arrangement.

       This information must be provided for customers to make informed business decisions on

the transmission service that best serves their operational and commercial needs. The decision to

take Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service or Interim NITS rather than full NITS is

fundamentally a commercial decision about the tradeoff between lower service costs and

potentially faster interconnection timelines and higher curtailment exposure. A co-located load



                                               12
 cannot make an informed decision without understanding how often and under what conditions

its service is likely to be interrupted. Without that information, the perceived risk of curtailment

will likely far outstrip the probable reality, and prospective customers will default to full NITS

simply to avoid uncertainty. The result would be exactly the opposite of what the Commission

intended: Rather than expanding the range of viable service options for co-located loads, the new

services would go largely unused.

        The Commission has long recognized that transparency is a prerequisite for competitive,

well-functioning markets. The same principle applies here. Just and reasonable rates, terms, and

conditions are not merely those that are technically correct on paper, they must be sufficiently

clear and transparent to enable customers to make informed decisions about whether and how to

participate.29 PJM’s curtailment framework, as proposed, does not meet that standard.

                 3. The Commission Should Direct PJM to Provide Curtailment
                    Transparency Mechanisms Prior to Implementation

        While uncertainty cannot be entirely avoided for customers selecting the Non-Firm

Contract Demand Transmission Service and Interim NITS, it can be minimized. The

Commission should direct PJM to take concrete steps to provide prospective customers with the

information they need to evaluate their curtailment exposure under Non-Firm Contract Demand

Transmission Service and Interim NITS before these services are implemented.

        First, the Commission should require PJM to resolve the “may/will” inconsistency in its

curtailment priority language and confirm the specific conditions under which Interim NITS and

Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service will be curtailed relative to pre-emergency

demand response dispatch and other system conditions.


29
  “Promoting Wholesale Competition Through Open Access Non-Discriminatory Transmission Services by Public
Utilities; Recovery of Stranded Costs by Public Utilities and Transmitting Utilities”, FERC Order No. 888, FERC
Stats. & Regs. ¶ 31,036, 61 Fed. Reg. 21,540 (1996).


                                                      13
            Second, the Commission should require PJM to develop and publish historical analysis

and forward-looking modeling of curtailment frequency and duration for Interim NITS and Non-

Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service, informed by historical system conditions in PJM

broken down by zone, where available. This analysis should be made available to prospective

customers and developers as part of the service application process so that they can evaluate their

curtailment exposure prior to committing to service.

           Third, PJM should dedicate time at a stakeholder meeting prior to implementation to

walk through the curtailment study process with a hypothetical co-located arrangement. This

exercise would give the market a concrete, practical understanding of how curtailment decisions

are made, what triggers them, and what a customer can expect in terms of frequency and duration

under a range of system conditions. As a predicate to that stakeholder engagement, PJM should

set out in its reply brief a written explanation of how it intends to operationalize curtailment for

Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service, including the criteria PJM will use to

determine when curtailment is warranted, the sequence in which co-located loads will be

curtailed relative to other non-firm services, and the mechanism by which curtailment

instructions will be communicated and enforced. Without that written explanation in this

proceeding and, ultimately, in PJM’s Business Practice Manuals, neither the Commission nor

affected parties can evaluate whether PJM's proposed curtailment framework is consistent with

the Co-Location Order’s requirement that Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service be

available “as needed during normal, non-emergency system operating conditions.”30 Greater

transparency at this stage will enable informed market participation and reduce the uncertainty

that would otherwise suppress uptake of these new services.



30
     Co-Location Order at P 215.


                                                  14
           PJM routinely gives market participants the information they need to evaluate the costs

and risks of participating in other PJM services,31 and the novelty of these new transmission

services makes the need for upfront transparency a necessity. The Commission should ensure

that PJM’s implementation plan includes these transparency measures so that Non-Firm Contract

Demand Transmission Service and Interim NITS can fulfill their intended purpose as genuinely

accessible, commercially viable alternatives to full NITS for co-located loads across the PJM

region.

             C. PJM Would Unnecessarily Subject All Co-Located Generating Facilities to a
                Full Interconnection Study.

          The Co-Location Order was designed to accelerate the integration of new load and new

generation into the PJM region at a time of unprecedented demand growth. PJM’s Brief

undermines that objective by proposing that all co-located generating facilities—including those

that have no intention of ever exporting power to the grid—must navigate the full PJM

interconnection queue before they can participate in Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission

Service or Interim NITS. While PJM indisputably requires sufficient information about both

exporting and non-exporting co-located generating facilities to reliably plan and operate the

transmission system, subjecting non-exporting resources to the full interconnection queue

imposes costs, delays, and administrative burdens that are wholly disproportionate to the

reliability benefits achieved. This outcome would further strain an interconnection queue that is

already significantly backlogged, all to the detriment of the broader PJM region and the

customers it serves.




31
  Such as the Base Residual Auction’s planning parameters and load forecasts, the interconnection queue with
cluster study reports and cost estimates, and historical dispatch data for demand response customers.


                                                       15
            PJM’s proposal appears to require all co-located generating facilities participating in the

new transmission services will be required to go through PJM’s interconnection queue, and it

acknowledges that this will contribute to delays in the availability of the new transmission

services. PJM states that “the process of an Eligible Customer's generation getting through the

interconnection queue, being constructed, and becoming operational will likely take more than

three years, particularly in light of current supply chain issues, Transmission Owner and PJM

queue requirements, and RPM auction timelines.”32 PJM makes no distinction between

generating facilities that intend to export power to the grid and those that are dedicated

exclusively to serving their co-located load.

           This one-size-fits-all approach is fundamentally misaligned with the purpose of the

interconnection queue and the objective of achieving speed-to-power. PJM’s interconnection

process was designed to study the deliverability and system impact of generating facilities that

intend to inject power into the transmission system and participate in PJM’s energy and capacity

markets. The interconnection studies include network upgrades analysis, deliverability

assessments, and capacity market participation determinations and are premised on the

assumption that the generator will export power to the grid and that the grid must be capable of

receiving and delivering that power to load. These assumptions do not apply to a non-exporting

co-located generating facility whose output is dedicated entirely to serving its co-located load

and that will never inject power into the system.

           Requiring non-exporting co-located generating facilities to undergo this process does not

make the transmission system more reliable, it simply foists multi-year delays and significant

costs on resources that pose none of the deliverability risks the interconnection queue was



32
     PJM Brief at 82.


                                                    16
 designed to address. As was argued in the related proceeding in Docket No. ER26-1479, non-

exporting resources “do not require deliverability given their intent to serve only the co-located

load” and will “rarely, if ever, trigger network upgrades,” making the full interconnection study

process a “purely administrative hurdle with no technical or reliability benefit.”33

        The consequences of PJM’s approach extend beyond the individual customer. PJM itself

acknowledges that its interconnection queue has been severely backlogged—it effectively closed

the queue to new applicants in 2022 and will not initiate the first cluster study of new requests

until later this year.34 Forcing non-exporting co-located generating facilities into that queue

would artificially inflate the number of projects competing for study resources and queue

positions, further delaying all projects in the queue, including the exporting generators whose

deliverability the interconnection process was actually designed to assess. This is precisely the

kind of outcome the Co-Location Order sought to avoid.

        The Co-Location Order’s objective is not merely a commercial convenience for

individual customers, it reflects the Commission’s recognition that the PJM region faces urgent

resource adequacy challenges that require new generation and new load to come online as

quickly as possible.35 Nevertheless, the Commission should not exempt non-exporting co-located

generating facilities from all study or registration requirements. PJM needs sufficient

information about these resources to model them accurately, ensure the reliability and stability of

the transmission system, and establish the necessary systems required under the new

transmission services. Those are legitimate operational needs.




33
   “Limited Protest of Advanced Energy United and the Solar Energy Industries Association,” Docket No. ER26-
1479-000, at 24 (Mar. 16, 2026).
34
   See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., PJM Completes Interconnection Reform Transition Cycle 1 Studies (Sept. 22,
2025), https://insidelines.pjm.com/pjm-completes-interconnection-reform-transition-cycle-1-studies/.
35
   Co-Location Order at P 200


                                                      17
         The Commission should instead direct PJM to develop a study and registration pathway

that is proportional to the actual technical impact that non-exporting resources have on the

transmission system. This process should provide PJM with the information it needs without

subjecting non-exporting resources to the full burdens of the interconnection queue. Such a

pathway could include, at a minimum, standardized submission of key technical data including

nameplate capacity, generation profile and operational parameters, a binding non-export

commitment enforceable through the service agreement, telemetry and metering capabilities

sufficient to support PJM's real-time operational visibility, and single-line diagram and delivery

point information. These requirements would give PJM the information it needs to reliably

incorporate non-exporting co-located generating facilities into its planning and operations

without the multi-year delays and costs associated with a full interconnection study.

        This approach is consistent with the Commission's broader policy of tailoring

interconnection requirements to the actual system impacts of the resource seeking

interconnection.36 It is also consistent with the position advanced in the related proceeding in

Docket No. ER26-1479, where United and SEIA explained that PJM should “establish a

streamlined, expedited process specifically for resources that do not intend to export to the grid”

with requirements “proportional to the actual technical impact the resources have on the grid.”37

This same logic has been used on other regions. In another proceeding Commissioner Rosner

highlighted SPP’s approach of limiting a generator’s grid output to match co-located load

demand as a model worth emulating because, when generation is matched to load, “the impacts

of adding load and generation to the transmission system effectively cancel each other out, which

             D. The Commission Should Direct PJM to Explicitly Allow Co-Located Loads
                Under New Transmission Service to Access On-site Generation During
                System Constraint Periods

         The Interim NITS as currently proposed leaves unclear whether co-located loads may

access on-site generation during system constraint periods. PJM’s brief outlines significant

operational complexities and restrictions for Co-Location but is unclear on the use of on-site

generation post-curtailment. This ambiguity creates uncertainty, which almost certainly will

deter loads from considering Interim NITS. To provide clarity, encourage fair access, and align

with the Commission’s Order, the Commission should direct PJM to explicitly allow co-located

loads employing Interim NITS to use on-site generation during system constraints.

         PJM is explicit that interim NITS will be among the first services curtailed during

emergencies and must be prepared to shed load when system reliability requires it.39

Additionally, Interim NITS may be curtailed prior to dispatching emergency programs.40 Given

the curtailment hierarchy, it is likely that interim NITS will be curtailed from the grid early and

often during system constraints to shed load and ensure reliability. However, it is unclear

Order, which clearly states: “when curtailed, Eligible Customers taking this transmission service

on behalf of Co-Located Loads may be able to continue to take energy from the Interconnection

Customer with which they are co-located if PJM’s Tariff otherwise allows.”42 If PJM intends to

restrict co-located loads from accessing on-site generation while using interim NITS, this would

be a fundamental flaw in the Interim NITS framework and a direct violation of the

Commission’s order.

        During system constraints, without clearer tariff language, co-located loads could be

restricted from both the grid and on-site generation to serve their load. This removes the benefit

of co-locating with a generator. On-site generation resources are critical tools for customers to

manage their energy needs and enhance reliability. One of the main benefits of the Interim NITS

option for co-located loads comes from being able to connect to on-site generation quickly while

still meeting reliability needs. The grid benefits from adding load that does not impact system

reliability, if the generation serving the load is new generation. While PJM's concern about

existing generation being repurposed to serve new loads is understandable, the proposed

framework would confine on-site generation resources during curtailment, undermining the

operational flexibility that Non-Firm Demand and Interim NITS should provide.

III.      CONCLUSION

          For the foregoing reasons, United and SEIA respectfully request that the Commission

find that PJM's initial brief does not fully satisfy the requirements of the Co-Location Order and

direct PJM to revise its proposed terms and conditions to address the deficiencies identified

herein. The Commission's prompt action on these issues is essential to ensure that the new

transmission services established by the Co-Location Order fulfill their intended purpose of

delivering reliable, flexible, and affordable energy service to co-located loads across the PJM

region.
